title: Sunny Deol Just Made His OTT Debut. Twenty-Nine Years After Border, He's Back With Akshaye Khanna.
excerpt: Ikka reunites two of Bollywood's most electrifying screen presences in a courtroom thriller on Netflix — and while the film divides critics, Sunny's emotional tribute to his late father Dharmendra might be the real story.
body:
Some reunions carry a weight that no script can fully contain. When **Sunny Deol** and **Akshaye Khanna** last shared a screen, it was 1997 and they were soldiers walking into a war that would become the defining film of a generation. **Border** didn't just make money — it became a cultural artefact, the kind of film whose dialogue still echoes through WhatsApp forwards and Independence Day rewatches.

Twenty-nine years later, they're back. Not on the battlefield, but in a courtroom. And not in theatres, but on **Netflix**.

**Ikka** marks Sunny Deol's long-awaited OTT debut, and the platform couldn't have chosen a more loaded premise. Directed by **Siddharth P. Malhotra**, the film casts Sunny as **Arjun Mehra** — a celebrated defence lawyer with a flawless courtroom record and a nickname that doubles as the title. His reputation is built on principles, not shortcuts. He's the kind of man who believes the law works, which is exactly the kind of belief that makes for good drama when it's tested.

The test arrives in the form of **Shauryaman Gaur**, played by Akshaye Khanna with the kind of coiled menace he's perfected over the last decade. Gaur is the son of a powerful politician, accused of murder, and the last man on earth Arjun Mehra would choose to defend. But choice has been taken off the table — Arjun's family is being held hostage, and the only way to get them back is to win the case.

> "Papa ke bete hai, aur kya hai? Accha kaam karte hai toh accha lagta hai ki papa khush honge." — Sunny Deol, at the Mumbai premiere, speaking about his late father Dharmendra

That quote, delivered at a special screening in Mumbai days before the release, says more about where Sunny Deol is right now than any film could. Both the teaser and trailer introduce him as **"Dharmendra's son Sunny Deol"** — a deliberate, emotional choice that honours a legacy while signalling that this isn't the Sunny of *Gadar* sequels and franchise obligations. This is personal.

## The Verdict Is Mixed — And That's Fine

Critics have been candid. **India Forums** gave it **2.5 out of 5**, calling it "a case that begins with compelling arguments but loses steam before the final verdict." The courtroom scenes lack urgency at times, the tone shifts between family drama and commercial entertainer without fully committing to either, and the much-anticipated Sunny-Akshaye face-off doesn't quite deliver the fireworks the reunion demanded.

But — and this matters — the film isn't bad. It's watchable. The central moral dilemma works. The mystery holds. And there's a performance hiding inside this film that deserves attention.

**Tillotama Shome**, playing prosecutor Madhura Banerjee, quietly steals every scene she's in. Where the leads oscillate between restraint and theatrical intensity, Shome stays grounded. She plays an everyday lawyer doing her job with conviction, and it's the kind of understated work that makes you wonder what this film could have been if the entire cast had been directed with her precision.

**Dia Mirza** brings warmth as Arjun's wife, though the script tantalisingly hints at a shared past between her character, Arjun, and Shauryaman that it never fully explores. It's the kind of emotional thread that, if pulled, could have elevated the entire second act.

## What Sunny Said at the Screening

At the Mumbai premiere, Sunny showed up clean-shaven in a checked shirt and jeans — a look that immediately sparked speculation about his role in Nitesh Tiwari's upcoming **Ramayana**. When someone asked about the industry's obsession with appearances, he laughed and said in Punjabi: *"Aaj kal te looks de pichhe paye jaande ne. Acting te khatam ho gayi hai."*

Translation: "Everyone's chasing looks these days. The art of acting is finished."

It's the kind of remark that sounds like a joke but lands like a thesis statement. In an era where leading men are more likely to be photographed at the gym than on a film set, Sunny Deol — with his lived-in face and unvarnished screen presence — is a reminder of what Bollywood used to prioritise.

## Where to Watch

**Ikka** is streaming now on **Netflix**, available in Hindi with subtitles. For the diaspora, this is the kind of low-stakes, two-hour watch that works on a weeknight — it won't change your life, but the reunion is worth showing up for, and Tillotama Shome alone is worth the price of your subscription.

Sunny's next is **Batwara 1947**, reuniting him with director **Rajkumar Santoshi** and marking his first collaboration with **Aamir Khan Productions**. That one arrives on August 14 — Independence Day weekend, because of course it does.

The courtroom may have been mixed. But Sunny Deol's second innings? It's just getting started.
